cells.tense: The ground is clear and the work is underway now, with both hands on it.
cells.ask: Take the next physical step on the thing today and tell one person what it is, so the making gets a witness instead of staying private.
cells.core:
The old arrangement is gone and what you're raising is new — your hands are on it and the course is set. At the bench you can tell what's real from what's still pretend, and you're choosing what to carry before you carry it. You don't need the whole shape to know the next piece belongs.

It's quieter than what it replaced. Nothing is being forced, and that isn't the same as nothing happening — the work goes on at a working pace. That steadiness is what's free to feed whatever comes next: it holds when the next piece gets hard. Let someone see the thing taking form; it's yours, and it's fine for it to be.
cells.sheetLine: You're raising something new and you know it's yours.

cells.tense: Most of you is standing in a finished version of this that hasn't been built yet, and the work keeps getting measured against it.
cells.ask: Pick the one piece the work actually needs next and do that piece alone today, letting the rest of the plan stay unwritten.
cells.core:
You can picture the end of this so clearly that the picture is where you're living — every plan gets checked against how you've imagined it landing, and every move has to close the gap in one stroke. Nothing in the middle counts unless it's the final version. Building doesn't move that way; it moves one course at a time, and the courses change as the ground does.

When it's going well, the thing that came out of the last clearing gets made by hand — piece fitted to piece, judged by what's in front of you. That's the honest pace, and it's available right now, not at the finish. Rushing ahead doesn't speed up the raising; it just puts the work somewhere the ground can't carry it yet.

cells.tense: You're still standing where the old arrangement came down, tools in hand, nothing raised on the cleared ground.
cells.ask: Lay out the first two pieces of the work today and tell one person the two sentences of why you chose them.
cells.core:
The clearing happened and the building didn't follow. When it's going well, this is a plain bench: you deal the first pieces onto it, name where each one goes, and leave them out so tomorrow starts where today stopped. Nothing announces itself; the work is the authority because it stays put.

What's missing isn't the plan — you know what you'd make, the shape of it is right there in your head. Declaring it and starting it have stayed in different rooms. Laying the first course is what pulls the current back; two pieces on the bench beat a framework described.

cells.tense: Your hands are on the work right now — the thing is being built as you sit here — and the claim that you're the one doing it has gone quiet.
cells.ask: Write down the one result you want the build to show by the end of the week, and say once that this is the course you're building.
cells.core:
It gets talked about as something happening to you — the schedule, the demands, the thing that came up — when it's your hands choosing the pace and the order. You build it, you sort the sequence, you decide what gets raised, and the credit for that goes somewhere else. When it's honest, the work comes out of wanting to make the thing itself: time at the bench that doesn't ask permission, and someone who chooses it on purpose.

That wanting is the current you're already in; naming where the direction comes from is the difference between being carried by the build and standing in it. This is the day it's moving. Say it's yours and the day stops moving without you.

attempts.check: One risk: 'the first structure raised by more than one pair of hands' points at collaboration the record doesn't establish about any actual project — so the cells stay with what can be done alone with two hands and don't claim a partner or a crew exists. A reader could say 'I'm not waiting on any cleared ground; nothing has been cleared' — the cells don't require a clearing, only work that didn't exist before the last thing ended. The asks are single acts — declare one course, take the next physical step — so they teach something even if the read is wrong. The line most in danger of serving the writer is 'this is the day it's moving' near the close of the last cell; it's kept because it says when, not who.
